one_liner: CUDA library and kernel driver that let GPU threads issue NVMe reads and writes themselves, bypassing CPU-orchestrated storage paths.
what_it_does: BaM (ASPLOS'23) maps NVMe submission and completion queues into GPU-visible memory so CUDA kernels can fetch data from SSDs on demand, without a CPU round trip per request. Applications use a header-only CUDA C++ layer in include/ (page_cache.h, bam_ptr, the bam::array abstraction) that checks a GPU-resident software cache and issues NVMe commands on a miss. This is a different interface, not a file API: the SSD is unbound from the Linux NVMe driver and accessed as raw blocks through a custom libnvm kernel module (/dev/libnvm*).
how_it_is_fast: GPU self-orchestrated storage access: thousands of GPU threads enqueue NVMe commands concurrently into many deep queues (128 queues x 1024 entries in the examples) using ticket-based lock-free submission (atomic fetch_add tickets in nvm_parallel_queue.h). A fine-grained GPU software cache with warp-level request coalescing (__match_any_sync) and round-robin slot allocation cuts I/O amplification, and PCIe peer-to-peer DMA moves data straight from SSD into GPU memory. The gain comes from removing CPU-GPU synchronization and staging for fine-grained, data-dependent access, not from faster per-request I/O.
when_to_use: Graph analytics (BFS, CC, SSSP, PageRank) or similar data-dependent workloads whose working set exceeds GPU memory and lives on NVMe
You control the whole box: x86 server with PCIe P2P, Volta-or-newer datacenter GPU (V100/A100/H100) and dedicated NVMe SSDs that can be detached from the OS
Research or prototyping on GPU-initiated I/O where cutting host memory and CPU cost (the paper reports up to 21.7x lower hardware cost) matters as much as speed
Fine-grained random reads (512 B to 4 KiB) from many GPU threads, where batching through cudaMemcpy or GPUDirect Storage would amplify I/O
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs a filesystem: BaM reads raw NVMe blocks on an SSD unbound from the kernel driver, so datasets must first be written with its readwrite tool
Consumer GPUs or Tesla T4 (256 MB BAR is too small), Arm servers (open enhancement request), AMD GPUs (no ROCm support), or VMs (open question)
Production systems: IOMMU and ACS must be disabled, tested on Linux 5.8.x, and the README warns 6.x kernels and post-20.04 Ubuntu P2P changes may break it
Streaming workloads with known access patterns, where CPU-pipelined transfers are already efficient; the paper's BFS result is parity (1.0x) in time
When you need the data-analytics path behind the 5.3x claim: that implementation is proprietary and not in the repo

integration.form: header-only (CUDA headers in include/) plus static lib (libnvm) and an out-of-tree kernel module
integration.dependencies: CUDA 12.3+, NVIDIA driver 440.33+ with compiled kernel symbols, CMake 3.10+ with FindCUDA, git submodules (freestanding, simt atomics), custom libnvm kernel module
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMake sets -std=c++11), GCC 5.4+, CUDA 12.3+; default GPU archs sm_70/80/90
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux (tested kernel 5.8.x) with PCIe P2P and Above 4G Decoding; NVIDIA Volta or newer datacenter GPU
integration.thread_safety: Designed for massive concurrency from GPU threads (atomic ticket queues, per-page atomic state); host-side thread safety not documented

gotchas: bam_ptr's operator[] marks cache pages dirty even on reads, so read-only kernels can trigger spurious NVMe writes (issue #56 saw about 35% writes on a Zipfian read benchmark); use seq_read() for reads
BaM writes to the raw SSD; the README warns not to keep any needed data on it
Open reports of segfaults and errors in nvm-block-bench (#37 and others), an illegal memory access in vectoradd, and inconsistent load/store after large data volumes
Graph datasets used in the paper are not public; you must ask the authors
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick BaM over SPDK or liburing only when the consumer of the data is a GPU kernel with data-dependent access: SPDK and io_uring keep the CPU in the I/O path, while BaM lets GPU threads drive the NVMe queues. For loading model weights into GPUs, fastsafetensors or InstantTensor are far easier to deploy.
verified_claims_summary: The README quotes the ASPLOS'23 abstract: BFS end-to-end parity (1.0x) and CC 1.49x versus CPU-orchestrated GPU storage access with up to 21.7x lower hardware cost, and 5.3x on proprietary data-analytics queries on the same hardware; compiler flags and CPU model for the paper runs are not on the page. The asplosaoe logs only show functional runs on the artifact machine (e.g. nvm-block-bench on one Intel Optane at 4.90M ops/s, 2.34 GB/s with 512 B requests; one Samsung 980 Pro at 0.80M ops/s, 3.05 GB/s with 4 KiB requests) with no baseline in the same log.
status_note: Active research artifact (last commit 2025-11-23, 17 open issues), BSD-2-Clause (inherited from Jonas Markussen's ssd-gpu-dma), copyable but tied to a narrow hardware and kernel setup.
